episode_thesis: A ten-manager year-end panel argues that (1) total-portfolio optimisation theoretically implies far larger CTA allocations than the roughly 50bp most US institutions hold, but flows follow performance and career risk, so TPA will not change much quickly; (2) the 2023-25 trend drawdown is explained by volatility compression and a share of winning markets below break-even, not by model failure, so managers should not change models after pain and should stay true to their stated thesis; (3) CTA drawdowns come from nothing happening, are long rather than deep, and are smaller than perceived; and (4) long volatility and trend following provide true diversification that stock-bond mixes do not. The panel also debates high-vol products, capital efficiency and 2026 predictions (higher yields, 2022-like, roller coaster).

speakers.name: Yoav Git
speakers.role: CTA manager (Israel); sells non-financialized trend risk factors
speakers.speaker_note: Ledger labels 'Yov'. Caption spelling varies. Assumed to be the speaker of C02, C07-C08 and C10-C11 per flow; turn boundaries rely on host cues.

worldview_premises.premise: Total-portfolio mean-variance optimisation implies a very large CTA allocation because of diversification (about 1/3 of risk even at CTA Sharpe 0.5 vs 1.5 for the rest), but flows follow performance, so TPA will not change allocations much.
worldview_premises.support: Simple optimisation arithmetic; observation that flows chase performance.

worldview_premises.premise: CTA exposure should be matched to hedge the asset classes an allocator already holds; bucket-style allocation leaves CTAs at ~2%, too small to alter convexity.

Recent CTA underperformance came from fewer outsized trends (volatility compression), not model breakdown; test it by measuring Sharpe extracted from markets that trended at a given underlying Sharpe versus history.
worldview_premises.support: Measurement logic; says it is roughly unchanged for most CTAs.

worldview_premises.premise: CTA drawdowns come from nothing happening, like buying straddles paid for via trading costs; only ~40% of markets need to win for a good year, and a drawdown comes when winners fall to 30-35%.
Drawdowns have no single event to blame, so they are harder for allocators to explain to an investment committee; they are long rather than deep.
A manager should stay true to the style the investor hired (e.g., non-financialized markets, fast trend) and change only when the underlying market properties change.
worldview_premises.support: Example: iron ore front month where ~70% of volume is CTAs.

worldview_premises.premise: AI is used cautiously (coding, summaries, testing message clarity), not in the models.

steps.from: Share of winning markets falls below break-even (~40% to 30-35%)
steps.to: Multi-year drawdown without a single deep loss
steps.why: Costs of straddle-like trading are not offset

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated; model breakdown test would show lower Sharpe extraction per unit of underlying trend.

decision_process.practice: Diagnose underperformance by measuring Sharpe extracted from trending markets versus history before touching the model.
decision_process.why: Separates model failure from fewer trends.

decision_process.practice: Drop markets that become financialized (e.g., CTAs ~70% of iron-ore front-month volume) because the product thesis is trading what others do not trade.
decision_process.why: Preserve the factor exposure the investor bought.

speakers.evidence_style: Industry experience and measurement logic; no data shown.

current_views.view: Most likely outcome for 2026: 10-year Treasury yield around 6%; he would wish for equities +25%.

speakers.name: Unnamed panelist (possibly Andrew Beer)
speakers.role: Panelist agreeing with Yoav on TPA
speakers.speaker_note: Ledger names Jim for C03-3/C03-4 but the transcript brings Jim in only at the end of C04; the speaker is unidentified (ledger correction). C04-X1 (breaking anchoring; theatre) also follows this speaker's turn.

worldview_premises.premise: In a strategic allocation managed futures merits ~25% because almost nothing else is scalable, liquid, zero-correlated to stocks and bonds and pays off when needed (pod shops come close).
worldview_premises.support: Statistical measures cited from the GIC/JPM paper.

worldview_premises.premise: US institutions hold ~6% in hedge funds with managed futures <10% of that (~50bp of the portfolio); career risk and benchmarking to hedge fund indices prevent moving it to ~30% of the sleeve.
TPA could break anchoring to indices and legacy bucket sizes by forcing a statistical blank sheet, though much of TPA is theatre to win broader mandates.

speakers.evidence_style: Statistical measures and observed allocator behaviour.

worldview_premises.premise: A hedge fund portfolio optimised within the total portfolio tilts to CTA, macro and commodities and away from equity long-short and credit, which duplicate held factors.
A trend program already behaves like a total portfolio approach because it dynamically allocates risk to the best risk-adjusted markets.
TPA has an unresolved look-through problem: investment teams making tactical views while allocating to managers who also make tactical bets.
High-vol trend managers repeat a cycle of exceptional years, asset gathering, deep drawdown and asset loss; a high-vol ETF would follow the same flow cycle.
Wealth portfolios should hold a balanced diversified portfolio and then lever to the desired risk rather than add equities.

current_views.view: 2026 will be the year of the bond breakout: US 10-year yields up to 6% then down to 3.5%.

speakers.name: Jim (volatility specialist; caption 'Jim Kasang')
speakers.role: Panelist focused on long volatility and portfolio construction
speakers.speaker_note: The ledger's C03 attributions are removed (not Jim). C12 attributions follow the host's cue 'perception of risk' after Katie.

worldview_premises.premise: 95% of investors diversify by holding more correlated assets; stocks and 60/40 each have about a 0.35 Sharpe over 125 years so bonds gave no Sharpe benefit; true diversification needs non-asset strategies such as trend and long volatility.
worldview_premises.support: Allocators he asked cannot name the Sharpe; the 0.35 figure is quoted from memory.

worldview_premises.premise: Academic research points to a long-volatility hedge as the one consistent diversifier and most important portfolio component.
worldview_premises.support: 'Tons of academic research' (uncited); David Dredge conversation.

worldview_premises.premise: The stock-bond structure dates from about 1985 and persists through recency bias and the long falling-rate era that removed the need to manage risk.
Distribution width and tail fatness by regime (volatility) are forecastable while direction is not, so trend-model choice should rest on a forward view of the distribution, not backtest optimisation.
Managed futures drawdown (~15-16% over 25 years) is small relative to equities, and bonds' recent 15-16% drawdown after 20 years undercuts the view that CTAs are riskier.
Trend following earns most when the world changes (inflation shock, regime shifts over ~24 months) and struggles in noisy markets that total-portfolio allocators with static assumptions handle badly.

mechanism_chains.topic: Long volatility as brakes on a race car

steps.from: Long vol earns about zero long-run
steps.to: Allocators remove it as a drag
Portfolio can keep risk on and accelerate on straights

mechanism_chains.evidence: Metaphor from David Dredge's conversation; no numbers.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why CTAs matter in a concentrated portfolio

steps.from: Portfolio concentrated in AI trade across equities, rates and more
Trend program cuts losers and can go short
steps.why: Disciplined loss-cutting vs narrative of conviction

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Noise year with no world change.

decision_process.practice: Choose trend model by forward view of return distribution (volatility regime, supply and demand) rather than backtest optimisation.
decision_process.why: Distribution is more predictable than direction.

speakers.evidence_style: Academic literature, metaphors and a few headline statistics from memory.

current_views.view: 2026 resembles 2022: pain trade is stocks down and rates up; implied-vol and VIX hedges could pay; rates higher hurts those holding bonds for diversification.
current_views.reasoning: Investors own stocks with long-vol bandaids and bonds as diversifier.

speakers.name: Andrew Beer
speakers.speaker_note: Ledger attribution used for C06-C07, C09, C13-C16.

worldview_premises.premise: A replication model left unchanged for ten years gives a fully consistent track record; the best outcome for an allocator is that the manager never needs changes, because it is hard to know whether changes help going forward.
A legitimate reason to revisit a model is evidence of industry-wide drift (all managers moving to 15-20 day models), visible against a benchmark or replication; without it do not change.
Slower and simpler trend models outperformed more complex ones over the last three years; managers should own the design decisions that cost return in this regime.
worldview_premises.support: Presented data (about 1,100bp cost used as illustration).

worldview_premises.premise: With wide dispersion and no persistence of alpha, allocators chase the recent winner and oversell it, producing a negative feedback loop when it underperforms.
ETF holders see price and drawdown every minute, so drawdowns matter; allocators trained to buy the dip want a rebound story that honest CTA managers cannot give.
Managed futures becomes a standard allocation if presented as a strategic long-term holding judged by portfolio benefit rather than lookbacks or positions.
worldview_premises.support: His stated thesis; to be tested in five years.

worldview_premises.premise: Higher interest rates make capital efficiency (return stacking, portable alpha, yield stacking) valuable again; 2x/3x growth reflects need for efficiency, not more risk.
The large pool of money is risk-averse allocators avoiding embarrassment, not leverage-seeking retail; niche ETF structures can reach multi-billion scale.

decision_process.practice: Change nothing in the model unless evidence of structural deviation; accept a very high bar for changes.
decision_process.why: Hard to tell whether changes help; consistent record is valuable.

speakers.evidence_style: Own track record, product experience and allocator observation.

current_views.view: Outrageous 2026: institutions begin buying managed futures ETFs (low probability, high significance).
current_views.reasoning: Allocators with 'hedge fund analyst' mandates look for hedge funds.

worldview_premises.premise: Managed futures drawdowns coincide with calm, equity-friendly, low-volatility environments, and recover faster when equity environments are challenging because hit ratio rises.
worldview_premises.support: Own paper on managed futures drawdowns (bubble chart).

worldview_premises.premise: After a very challenging period, one or two strong years typically followed; manager top/bottom timing is trend-following-trend.
worldview_premises.support: Fund-of-funds studies; mean reversion over longer horizons.

worldview_premises.premise: A daily-liquid high-vol CTA product cannot smooth prints as private equity does, so it will attract performance chasing and disappoint, as with Bitcoin; institutional adoption pushed managers to lower risk and size management.

current_views.view: 2026 will be a boom-and-bust roller coaster: rates fall and over-stimulation make conditions look strong before things fall apart.
current_views.reasoning: Something brewing in the macro change of 2025.

worldview_premises.premise: Markets change but process should not change in response to recent outcomes; a stable process does not remove drawdowns but prevents panic and rule changes (the main investor mistake).
worldview_premises.support: Own practice; asks panel how much change is evolution vs reaction to pain.

decision_process.practice: Pre-commit to a stable process; explain to allocators how the strategy behaves in uncomfortable conditions.
decision_process.why: Stability builds trust and prevents behavioral drift.

worldview_premises.premise: Drawdowns are a prompt to review for blind spots but not a reason to change the model, especially when explained by repeated V-shaped reversals (yen, Liberation Day).
A replication of the CTA index need not change when underlying managers change models as long as the changes net out and managers do not become too fast to track.
A benchmark model need not minimise tracking error; high tracking error in a year does not show the model works or fails.

decision_process.practice: Treat pain as invitation to reflect, not to change.

worldview_premises.premise: A Sharpe-1 strategy run at half Kelly implies roughly 40-50% annualised volatility, so high-vol CTA products are feasible and could be sold to retail with fees proportional to volatility.

decision_process.practice: Half Kelly sizing for a Sharpe-near-1 strategy.
decision_process.why: Maximise growth with a safety margin.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Speaker attribution is uncertain for C03-C04 (Jim vs unnamed panelist), C07 (Yoav vs others) and the host question turns; ledger corrections applied.
The 25% and ~1/3 optimal-allocation claims rest on stated Sharpe and correlation assumptions (Sharpe 0.5 vs 1.5, zero correlation) that are not demonstrated.
Stock/60-40 Sharpe of 0.35 over 125 years is quoted from memory; no source given.
Volatility compression as the sole cause of 2023-25 underperformance is argued from a Sharpe-extraction test that is described but not shown.
Andrew says changes are rarely helpful; Jim and Yoav propose forward-looking or thesis-driven adaptation, so 'never change' vs 'adapt to distribution' is not reconciled.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs named: share of markets winning (40% vs 30-35%), Sharpe extracted per unit of underlying trend, volatility compression, front-month CTA share of volume (financialisation), stock-bond correlation, rates and inflation regimes, manager dispersion and index volatility. Horizons: multi-year drawdowns recover over 1-2 years after challenging periods; 2026 views are annual.
reader_inferences: (reader) The panel's shared claim is that drawdown diagnosis should separate trend availability from model quality; this suggests a monitoring metric (winner share, Sharpe extraction) for the book.
(reader) Several speakers (Jim, Yoav, Allan) converge on trend and long volatility as complements; only Jim attaches an explicit 2026 trade.
(reader) The predictions segment is flagged by the host as 'outrageous', so treat 2026 views as low-confidence.
